looking for when I wrote this note.

The observation that the number happened, Wheeler's delayed choice
experiment might suggest.

-----Original Message-----
From: nhi-pljlbix@engr.orst.edu [mailto:nhi-pljlbix@engr.orst.edu] On
Behalf Of Rich
Sent: Saturday, August 26, 2006 11:06 AM
To: Kathryn Blackmond Laskey; Doug Morgan; Kathryn Blackmond Laskey
Cc: faq@engr.orst.edu
Subject: Re: [UAI] Determinism verses chance

Dear Kathy,

I think Doug pretty much articulated my position. You (Kathy) said the
following (in reverse order):

KATHY:

"But a meaningful definition of "full knowledge" for a probability
assessment would have to include only events occurring at times before
the event in question. I suspect Caves doesn't see any non-subjective
way to define "full prior knowledge" in a universe where temporal
relationships between events are relative.  But there is a meaningful,
observer-independent definition of "before", according to which we can
specify what "full knowledge" for quantum probability assessments should
mean.  In a universe subject to relativity theory, full prior knowledge
means everything in the past light cone of the event.  That is, quantum
theory predicts a probability for the state of a system immediately
after a measurement is performed, conditional on the measurement
operator that was applied and the entire past light cone of the system
at the instant of measurement.
So are quantum probabilities objective?

Einstein didn't think so. Jaynes didn't think so.  They both believed
that quantum probabilities reflect ignorance of some more fundamental
deterministic theory.  Despite considerable effort, no one has yet found
such a theory.  But people haven't stopped trying."

ME AGAIN:

The important point to me is that, based on everything E that happens up
to some point in time, something R ends up happening at the next
instant. If that event is not deterministically determined by E, then
what does determine it? That is, it seems to me that something made it
happen. Even if it is some random number generator that determines what
happens next, it seems that generator must generate its number right
before R occurred. So its result is part of E, and E determines R. Now
consider the event R' that this particular number was generated.
Everything  E' that occurred before R' determines R', and we see that we
can regress back in time indefinitely. We conclude that the events up
until now were deterministically produced. I have a hard time conceiving
of anything else, and I guess Einstein and Jaynes did also. The
alternative is that the number just `happens', but what does that mean?
A philosophical stance on what `just happens' could mean is what I was
looking for when I wrote this note.

This is why I feel that perhaps humans are too unevolved to grasp
determinism/indeterminism. We can grasp just enough to torment ourselves
with the notion. Just as the we can model more of external reality
(assuming one exists) than the amoeba, perhaps some future species will
do much better than us.

Rich
